newsitem.title: Egypt: Gas deal sidelines Israel at Mideast conference.
newsitem.headline: Gas deal sidelines Israel at Mideast conference.

text.p: Egypt, Turkey and the U.S. oil company Amoco signed on Wednesday a billion-dollar gas deal which sidelined an alternative project involving Israel.

The memorandum of understanding signed at the Middle East and North Africa Conference is for Egypt to export liquefied natural gas to Turkey by tanker at a project cost of between $2 billion and $4 billion.
Until only last month, the favoured alternative was a "peace pipeline" running from northeastern Egypt to Turkey by land through the Gaza Strip, Israel, Lebanon and Syria.

But Amoco's apparent frustration with the slow pace of the peace process as well as Egyptian impatience with Israel's lack of progress on the project persauded the U.S. oil giant to go for direct exports to Turkey as the quickest feasible solution.
"In Egypt we cannot wait and talk on speculation. So when we see something concrete from the Israeli side we will work with it," Egyptian Oil Minister Hamdi el-Banbi told a news conference.

While no official was willing to describe the decision as a snub to Israel, it reflected how this conference was focused on improving the environment for business in individual Middle East countries rather than cooperation with Israel.
Delegates said the change, which marked out the meeting in Cairo from its predecessors in Amman in 1995 and Casablanca in 1994, was caused by the Israeli elections in May.
They brought to power the rightwing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with reservations about the commitments made in the previous three years of peace talks.

"The fear at Casablanca and at Amman was that economic cooperation might lag behind the politics of peace. Unfortunately we do not have that fear today," said Yves Galland, head of the French delegation to the conference.
This has pushed Israel to the sidelines, though few of the Arab countries in Cairo have yet gone so far as to exclude the Jewish state from all of their plans.

"Casablanca was designed in the wrong way," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told a news conference. "Now we have it the correct way. Israel is just another country. We are telling Israel that its days of big talking are over."
"We are going ahead with our plans, regardless of what the Israelis are saying. We will not let the region be held hostage to Israeli policies," he added.
The Israelis have put a brave face on their marginalisation, while welcoming what they see as a focus on business.
"Casablanca was 90 percent political and the business people were just the decoration around the political bowl," said Dan Propper, president of the Manufacturers' Association of Israel.

"Amman was more business-oriented and in Cairo we can say that the messages we are hearing have been economic messages. The next meeting should be the same -- how to make the regional environment more friendly to business," he added.
Amoco was keen to stress that its memorandum of understanding with Turkey's Botas and Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation did not slam the door on projects involving Israel or other companies.
"This is not an exclusive project that is to say we will continue to look at other options to export Egyptian gas," said William Lowrie, president of Amoco Corp.
